notes:
1. Meaning of Political Party

  • A Political Party is an organised group of citizens who share common political principles and seek to acquire political power through constitutional and democratic means.

Political parties contest elections with the objective of:

  • Forming Government.
  • Influencing public policy.
  • Representing people's interests.

They act as a bridge between:

  • Government.
  • Legislature.
  • People.

2. Edmund Burke — Political Party

Political thinker:

  • Edmund Burke
  • described a political party as a group united around certain principles for promoting the national interest through collective action.
📌 Must-Memorise

Edmund Burke → Political Party

3. Objectives of Political Parties

Political parties seek to:

  • Contest elections.
  • Form Government.
  • Implement policies.
  • Represent public opinion.
  • Promote national development.
  • Maintain political stability.
  • Ensure democratic governance.

4. Development of the Party System

Major stages include:

  • Indian National Congress → 1885.
  • Muslim League → 1906.
  • Growth of Socialist parties.
  • Growth of Communist parties.
  • Rise of regional parties.
  • Increasing coalition politics after 1989.
  • Expansion of multi-party democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

1885 → Indian National Congress 1906 → Muslim League After 1989 → Coalition Politics became increasingly important

5. Multi-Party System

India follows a:

  • Multi-Party System.

Several political parties compete for political power at:

  • National level.
  • State level.

6. Why India Has a Multi-Party System

India's multi-party system reflects:

  • Social diversity.
  • Linguistic diversity.
  • Regional aspirations.
  • Federal structure.
  • Different political ideologies.
  • Democratic pluralism.

7. Characteristics of Political Parties

A political party generally possesses:

  • Organised membership.
  • Political leadership.
  • Common ideology.
  • Political programme.
  • Election strategy.
  • Party Constitution.
  • Public support.
  • Constitutional methods.
  • Desire to acquire political power.

8. Contest Elections

Political parties:

  • Select candidates.
  • Conduct campaigns.
  • Publish election manifestos.
  • Mobilise voters.
  • Offer electoral choices.

9. Form Government

A political party or coalition possessing sufficient legislative support forms:

  • Government.

It then attempts to implement its:

  • Manifesto.
  • Policies.
  • Development programmes.

10. Opposition

Political parties not forming Government constitute:

  • Opposition.

The Opposition:

  • Questions Government.
  • Examines policies.
  • Criticises Government decisions.
  • Suggests alternatives.
  • Represents alternative viewpoints.
  • Strengthens accountability.

11. Policy Formulation

Political parties formulate:

  • Manifestos.
  • Development programmes.
  • Legislative proposals.
  • Public policies.

12. Representation of Public Opinion

Political parties communicate:

  • People's demands.
  • Public grievances.
  • Regional aspirations.
  • Social interests.
  • Economic concerns
  • to Government and Legislature.

13. Political Recruitment

Political parties recruit and develop:

  • Political leaders.
  • Election candidates.
  • Legislators.
  • Ministers.
  • Future leadership.

14. Political Education

Political parties educate citizens about:

  • Elections.
  • Government policies.
  • Constitutional values.
  • Political issues.
  • Public affairs.

15. Political Participation

Political parties encourage citizens to:

  • Vote.
  • Contest elections.
  • Join public life.
  • Participate in debates.
  • Participate in democratic processes.

16. Peaceful Transfer of Power

Electoral competition among political parties facilitates:

  • Peaceful change of Government.
  • Democratic continuity.
  • Constitutional transfer of political authority.

17. National Integration

Responsible political parties can promote:

  • National unity.
  • Constitutional values.
  • Federal cooperation.
  • Peaceful competition.
  • Representation of diverse communities.

18. One-Party System

In a One-Party System:

  • One political party dominates or monopolises political power.
  • Political competition is severely limited or absent.

19. Two-Party System

In a Two-Party System:

  • Two major parties dominate electoral politics.
  • Governments generally alternate between them.

20. Multi-Party System

In a Multi-Party System:

  • Several political parties compete.
  • No single party is guaranteed dominance.
  • Coalition Governments may arise.

India follows:

  • Multi-Party System.

21. Advantages of Multi-Party System

Advantages include:

  • Wider representation.
  • Greater electoral choice.
  • Better regional representation.
  • Inclusive governance.
  • Accommodation of diverse interests.

22. Limitations of Multi-Party System

Possible limitations include:

  • Political fragmentation.
  • Coalition instability.
  • Frequent alliances.
  • Policy uncertainty.
  • Coalition pressure by smaller parties.

23. Meaning of Registration

Registration means:

  • Formal registration of a political party with the Election Commission of India.

24. Registration Authority

Political parties are registered by:

  • Election Commission of India.

The ECI confirms that registration is governed by:

  • Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
📌 Must-Memorise

Political Party Registration → ECI Section 29A → RPA, 1951

25. Registration vs Recognition

Registration:

  • Formal enrolment with ECI.
  • Does not automatically make a party a National or State Party.

Recognition:

  • Official status as National Party or State Party.
  • Granted after satisfying prescribed electoral criteria.

26. Core Recognition Rule

Every recognised political party is:

  • Registered.

But every registered political party is:

  • Not necessarily recognised.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Recognised → Registered Registered ≠ Automatically Recognised

27. Recognised Parties

The Election Commission recognises political parties as:

  • National Parties.
  • State Parties.

Recognition is governed principally by:

  • Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.

28. National Political Party

A National Party is a political party recognised by:

  • Election Commission of India
  • as satisfying the prescribed conditions for National Party status.

29. State Political Party

A State Party is recognised by:

  • Election Commission of India
  • for satisfying prescribed conditions within a particular State.

53. Current-Status Caution

  • Party recognition is not permanently fixed.

The Election Commission may:

  • Grant recognition.
  • Withdraw recognition.
  • Review recognition
  • according to electoral performance and the Election Symbols Order.

Therefore, National and State Party lists should always be treated as:

  • Current Affairs + Polity facts.

54. Meaning of Election Symbol

Election symbols are:

  • Visual identifiers allotted to political parties and candidates by Election Commission of India.

They help:

  • Identify candidates.
  • Reduce voter confusion.
  • Facilitate voting.

55. Types of Symbols

Election symbols are broadly:

  • Reserved Symbols.
  • Free Symbols.

56. Reserved Symbol

Reserved Symbols are associated with:

  • Recognised National Parties.
  • Recognised State Parties
  • within the applicable recognition framework.

57. Free Symbol

Free Symbols may be allotted to:

  • Registered Unrecognised Political Parties.
  • Independent candidates
  • according to ECI rules.

58. Election Symbols Order

Election-symbol recognition and allotment are governed by:

  • Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.
📌 Must-Memorise

Election Symbols Order → 1968

59. Article 324

Article 324 vests the:

  • Superintendence.
  • Direction.
  • Control

of elections in:

  • Election Commission of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 324 → Election Commission of India

60. ECI Functions Relating to Political Parties

The Election Commission:

  • Registers political parties.
  • Recognises National Parties.
  • Recognises State Parties.
  • Allots election symbols.
  • Resolves symbol disputes.
  • Conducts elections.
  • Supervises electoral processes.
  • Enforces electoral norms.

61. Meaning

The Model Code of Conduct is implemented by:

  • Election Commission of India
  • during elections.

62. Areas Covered by MCC

It contains guidelines regarding:

  • Election campaigning.
  • Public meetings.
  • Government announcements.
  • Use of official machinery.
  • Conduct of political parties.
  • Conduct of candidates.

63. Nature of MCC

The source notes that the MCC:

  • Is not itself a law separately enacted by Parliament.
  • Operates through ECI directions along with applicable election laws.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MCC → ECI Election Guidelines Not → Separate Parliamentary Act

64. Meaning of Coalition Politics

Coalition Politics means:

  • Two or more political parties joining together to form Government.

65. When Coalitions Arise

Coalitions commonly arise when:

  • No single political party obtains a majority in Legislature.

66. Pre-Poll Coalition

A Pre-Poll Coalition is formed:

  • Before elections.
  • Parties agree to cooperate before voters cast their votes.

67. Post-Poll Coalition

A Post-Poll Coalition is formed:

  • After election results

to obtain:

  • Legislative majority.

68. Common Minimum Programme

Coalition partners may adopt a:

  • Common Minimum Programme.

It contains:

  • Agreed policy priorities.
  • Common governing programme.

69. Advantages of Coalition Politics

Coalition Government may:

  • Represent diverse interests.
  • Increase regional representation.
  • Promote consensus.
  • Strengthen federalism.
  • Encourage political cooperation.

70. Limitations of Coalition Politics

Coalitions may face:

  • Political instability.
  • Policy delays.
  • Internal disagreement.
  • Coalition pressure.
  • Withdrawal of support.

71. Meaning

The Anti-Defection Law seeks to discourage:

  • Political defections by elected legislators.

It aims to promote:

  • Government stability.
  • Party discipline.
  • Protection of electoral mandate.

72. Constitutional Basis

The Anti-Defection Law is contained in:

  • Tenth Schedule.

73. Fifty-Second Amendment

The Tenth Schedule was inserted by:

  • Constitution (52nd Amendment) Act, 1985.
📌 Must-Memorise

52nd Amendment → 1985 → Tenth Schedule

74. Ninety-First Amendment

The Anti-Defection framework was strengthened by:

  • Constitution (91st Amendment) Act, 2003.

75. Important Changes under 91st Amendment

The Amendment:

  • Strengthened Anti-Defection Law.
  • Removed the earlier split exception.
  • Limited size of Councils of Ministers.
  • Restricted certain defectors from holding ministerial office.

76. Voluntarily Giving Up Membership

A member may be disqualified if:

  • The member voluntarily gives up membership of the political party.

77. Voting against Party Direction

A member may also face disqualification when:

  • Voting.
  • Abstaining from voting
  • contrary to party direction without permission and where the conduct is not condoned within the prescribed period.

78. Independent Members

An Independent Member is governed by special Tenth Schedule provisions concerning:

  • Joining a political party after election.

79. Nominated Members

Nominated Members are also subject to:

  • Special provisions regarding political-party membership under Tenth Schedule.

80. Authority to Decide Disqualification

Disqualification questions are decided by:

  • Speaker → Lok Sabha/Legislative Assembly.
  • Chairman → Rajya Sabha/Legislative Council.

81. Judicial Review

The decision of Speaker or Chairman under the Tenth Schedule is:

  • Subject to Judicial Review.

82. Criticisms of Anti-Defection Law

Major criticisms include:

  • Reduced independence of legislators.
  • Increased party-leadership control.
  • Delay in deciding petitions.
  • Reduced freedom for independent legislative voting.

83. Meaning

Political Party Funding refers to:

  • Financial resources received by parties for organisational and electoral activities.

84. Sources of Funding

The source identifies lawful sources such as:

  • Membership fees.
  • Individual contributions.
  • Corporate contributions subject to law.
  • Other lawful donations.
  • Electoral Bonds during the period in which the scheme operated.

85. Importance of Transparency

Funding transparency helps:

  • Reduce corruption.
  • Improve accountability.
  • Increase public confidence.
  • Improve electoral fairness.

86. Electoral Bond Scheme

The Electoral Bond Scheme was introduced in:

  • 2018.

87. Nature of Electoral Bonds

It operated as a mechanism for:

  • Political donations through banking channels.

  • Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, 2024,

the Supreme Court held:

  • Electoral Bond Scheme unconstitutional.
📌 Must-Memorise

ADR 2024 → Electoral Bonds Unconstitutional

89. Electoral Bonds Judgment — Importance

The judgment strengthened:

  • Political-funding transparency.
  • Electoral accountability.
  • Voters' access to relevant information.

90. Meaning

Inner-Party Democracy refers to:

  • Democratic functioning within political parties.

91. Elements

It includes:

  • Internal party elections.
  • Transparent leadership selection.
  • Member participation.
  • Democratic decision-making.
  • Internal accountability.

92. Importance

Inner-party democracy can:

  • Reduce concentration of power.
  • Promote accountability.
  • Develop new leadership.
  • Increase member participation.
  • Improve transparency.

93. Criminalisation of Politics

A major challenge is participation of persons facing:

  • Serious criminal allegations.

This may affect:

  • Public confidence.
  • Democratic credibility.
  • Ethical governance.

94. Money Power

High election expenditure can create:

  • Unequal electoral competition.
  • Dependence on wealthy donors.
  • Excessive influence of money.

95. Muscle Power

Use of:

  • Violence.
  • Threats.
  • Coercion.
  • Intimidation

undermines:

  • Free and fair elections.

96. Dynastic Politics

Concentration of leadership within political families may reduce:

  • Internal competition.
  • Leadership opportunities.
  • Merit-based advancement.
  • Party democracy.

97. Weak Inner-Party Democracy

Problems may include:

  • Limited internal elections.
  • Centralised leadership.
  • Weak transparency.
  • Limited member participation.

98. Defections

Political defections may:

  • Destabilise Governments.
  • Distort electoral mandates.
  • Reduce public confidence.

99. Identity Politics

Irresponsible mobilisation around:

  • Caste.
  • Religion.
  • Region.
  • Language

may weaken:

  • National integration.
  • Social harmony.

100. Digital Misinformation

Political use of digital platforms may involve:

  • Fake news.
  • Misinformation.
  • Hate speech.
  • Manipulated content.

101. Financial Opacity

Weak funding disclosure may:

  • Reduce public confidence.
  • Encourage corruption.
  • Distort electoral competition.

102. Reform Measures

Political parties can be strengthened through:

  • Greater transparency.
  • Internal democracy.
  • Ethical leadership.
  • Transparent political funding.
  • Effective electoral reforms.
  • Stronger enforcement of election laws.
  • Political education.
  • Responsible digital campaigning.
  • Greater citizen participation.

103. Electoral Reforms

Important reforms identified in the source include:

  • Candidate criminal-record disclosure.
  • Asset disclosure.
  • Liability disclosure.
  • Election expenditure monitoring.
  • EVMs.
  • VVPAT.
  • Voter-awareness programmes.
  • Funding transparency.
  • Model Code enforcement.

104. No Express Constitutional Definition

The Constitution:

  • Does not expressly define Political Party.

However, political parties are indispensable to:

  • Parliamentary democracy.
  • Representative Government.
  • Elections.
  • Responsible Government.

105. Article 19(1)(a)

Article 19(1)(a) guarantees:

  • Freedom of Speech and Expression.

Political parties exercise political expression through:

  • Campaigning.
  • Manifestos.
  • Speeches.
  • Public debate.

106. Article 19(1)(c)

Article 19(1)(c) guarantees:

  • Freedom to form Associations or Unions or Cooperative Societies.
  • It provides an important constitutional basis for voluntary political organisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 19(1)(c) → Freedom of Association

107. Article 324

Article 324:

  • Election Commission of India.
  • Superintendence, direction and control of elections.

108. Article 325

Article 325 provides for:

  • One General Electoral Roll.

No person may be excluded solely on grounds such as:

  • Religion.
  • Race.
  • Caste.
  • Sex.

109. Article 326

Article 326 provides:

  • Universal Adult Suffrage.

110. Article 327

Article 327 empowers:

  • Parliament

to legislate concerning:

  • Elections.
  • Electoral rolls.
  • Constituencies.
  • Conduct of elections.

111. Article 328

Article 328 empowers:

  • State Legislatures

to legislate regarding State elections subject to:

  • Constitution.
  • Parliamentary legislation.

112. Article 329

  • Article 329 restricts ordinary judicial interference in the electoral process.

Election disputes are generally resolved through:

  • Election Petitions
  • under the prescribed legal framework.

RPA, 1950 mainly deals with:

  • Electoral rolls.
  • Voter-related electoral framework.
  • Electoral administration.

  • Conduct of elections.
  • Political-party registration.
  • Candidate qualifications.

  • Election offences.

RPA 1950:

  • Electoral rolls.
  • Voters.

RPA 1951:

  • Conduct of elections.
  • Candidates.
  • Political parties.
  • Election disputes.

133. Political Party vs Pressure Group

Political Party:

  • Contests elections.
  • Seeks political power.
  • Forms Government.
  • Has broad political programme.

Pressure Group:

  • Mainly seeks to influence Government.
  • Normally does not seek to form Government.
  • Usually focuses on specific interests.

134. Ruling Party vs Opposition

Ruling Party:

  • Forms Government.
  • Implements policies.
  • Exercises executive authority.

Opposition:

  • Scrutinises Government.
  • Offers alternatives.
  • Questions policies.
  • Strengthens accountability.

135. Registered vs Recognised Party

Registered Party:

  • Registered with ECI.
  • May remain unrecognised.

Recognised Party:

  • Meets ECI recognition criteria.
  • Receives National or State Party status.

136. Reserved vs Free Symbol

Reserved Symbol:

  • Associated with recognised political party.

Free Symbol:

  • Available for eligible unrecognised parties and independent candidates.

137. Coalition vs Single-Party Government

Coalition Government:

  • Multiple parties.
  • Shared political power.
  • Consensus-oriented.
  • May face instability.

Single-Party Government:

  • One party forms Government.
  • More concentrated political authority.
  • Usually greater decisional coherence.

138. Political Funding vs Election Expenditure

Political Funding:

  • Money received by political parties.

Election Expenditure:

  • Money spent during election campaigns.

139. Inner-Party vs Parliamentary Democracy

Inner-Party Democracy:

  • Democracy within political party.

Parliamentary Democracy:

  • Democratic relationship between Legislature and Executive under Constitution.

140. Article 324 vs RPA 1951

Article 324:

  • Constitutional authority of ECI.

RPA 1951:

  • Statutory framework governing election conduct, candidates and political parties.

What is a Political Party? → An organised group of citizens sharing political principles and seeking political power through constitutional and democratic means.

Who gave a famous definition of Political Party? → Edmund Burke.

Which party system does India follow? → Multi-Party System.

Why does India have a Multi-Party System? → Social diversity, federalism, regional aspirations and democratic pluralism.

When was Indian National Congress formed? → 1885.

When was Muslim League formed? → 1906.

What are the major functions of political parties? → Contest elections, form Government, act as Opposition, formulate policies, represent public opinion, recruit leaders and promote political participation.

Who registers political parties? → Election Commission of India.

Under which provision? → Section 29A of Representation of the People Act, 1951.

What is Registration? → Formal enrolment of political party with ECI.

What is Recognition? → Official National or State Party status granted by ECI.

Is every registered party recognised? → No.

Is every recognised party registered? → Yes.

Which Order governs recognition and symbols? → Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.

What is a Reserved Symbol? → Symbol reserved for a recognised political party.

What is a Free Symbol? → Symbol available to eligible unrecognised parties and independent candidates.

Which Article deals with Election Commission? → Article 324.

What does Article 324 vest in ECI? → Superintendence, direction and control of elections.

What is MCC? → Model Code of Conduct.

Is MCC a Parliamentary Act? → No.

What is Coalition Politics? → Two or more political parties joining together to form Government.

What is a Pre-Poll Coalition? → Alliance formed before election.

What is a Post-Poll Coalition? → Alliance formed after election results.

What is Common Minimum Programme? → Agreed common governing programme of coalition partners.

What is Anti-Defection Law? → Constitutional mechanism designed to discourage legislators from changing political allegiance.

Where is Anti-Defection Law contained? → Tenth Schedule.

Which Amendment introduced it? → 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.

Which Amendment strengthened it? → 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.

Who decides disqualification in Lok Sabha or Legislative Assembly? → Speaker.

Who decides it in Rajya Sabha or Legislative Council? → Chairman.

Are these decisions subject to Judicial Review? → Yes.

Which case upheld Anti-Defection Law? → Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu, 1992.

What is Political Party Funding? → Financial resources received by parties for organisational and electoral purposes.

When was Electoral Bond Scheme introduced? → 2018.

Which case struck down Electoral Bonds? → Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, 2024.

What is Inner-Party Democracy? → Democratic functioning within a political party.

What does it include? → Internal elections, transparent leadership selection, member participation and democratic decision-making.

What are the major challenges faced by political parties? → Criminalisation, money power, muscle power, dynastic politics, weak internal democracy, defections, identity politics, misinformation and financial opacity.

Does the Constitution expressly define Political Parties? → No.

Which Article protects political speech? → Article 19(1)(a).

Which Article protects formation of associations? → Article 19(1)(c).

Which Article provides One General Electoral Roll? → Article 325.

Which Article provides Universal Adult Suffrage? → Article 326.

Which Article empowers Parliament to make election laws? → Article 327.

Which Article empowers State Legislatures regarding State election laws? → Article 328.

Which Article deals with bar on ordinary judicial interference in elections? → Article 329.

What does RPA 1950 mainly deal with? → Electoral rolls and voters.

What does RPA 1951 mainly deal with? → Conduct of elections, political parties, candidates, disqualifications and election disputes.

Which case is associated with Floor Test and Secularism? → S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994.

Which case directed candidate disclosure? → Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms, 2002.

Which case reaffirmed voters' Right to Know? → PUCL v. Union of India, 2003.

Which case struck down Section 8(4) of RPA 1951? → Lily Thomas v. Union of India, 2013.

Which case is associated with VVPAT? → Subramanian Swamy v. Election Commission of India, 2013.

Which case dealt with criminalisation of politics? → Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India, 2018.

Which Committee is associated with electoral reforms in 1974–75? → Tarkunde Committee.

Which Committee was established in 1990 for electoral reforms? → Dinesh Goswami Committee.

Which Committee recommended partial State Funding of Elections? → Indrajit Gupta Committee, 1998.

Which Law Commission report dealt with Inner-Party Democracy and Political Funding? → 170th Report.

Which Commission reviewed constitutional and political reforms in 2002? → National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution.

What is the easiest final memory line? → Political parties connect citizens with Government; Article 324 gives ECI constitutional authority over elections; Section 29A of RPA 1951 governs party registration; the Election Symbols Order 1968 governs recognition and symbols; and the Tenth Schedule regulates political defection.
